paragraphs.text: A new English rendering of our liturgy for the most sacred days of the year obviously requires a word of introduction. The Hebrew text on which this present attempt is based, will be familiar to those who follow the German rite; and it might well be regarded as a form of perpetuation of the memory of our blessed martyrs that their own particular liturgy should have survived intact in far-flung areas of the English-speaking world.

My aim has been to combine intelligibility with dignity in contemporary English. Archaisms have been avoided wherever possible. For instance, the archaic second person singular is reserved for the Divine and the normal second person plural of current usage applied to human beings. With regard to interpretation, the German translation of the late Rabbi Dr. Selig Bamberger of Hamburg has been closely followed throughout the numerous passages of mediaeval poetry, which depend so largely on Scriptural and Aggadic allusions.
Finally, I must acknowledge my gratitude to my husband and the many friends who have been generous with their help and advice.
